identity.title: Dual-mode biosensing featuring fluorescence and electrochemiluminescence for regional resolution of single-nucleotide variants.

content.abstract: Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) are a critical molecular basis for antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria. However, precise detection of mutant targets remains challenging because they may exist at low abundance and often coexist with wild-type sequences in complex biological matrices. Herein, we report a target-triggered strand displacement reaction that releases two functional DNA strands: one activates the trans-cleavage activity of CRISPR/Cas12a to generate a fluorescent signal, while the other competitively displaces cadmium sulfide quantum dots pre-modified on a gold electrode surface, decreasing the electrochemiluminescence (ECL) signal. The two functional strands hybridize to distinct regions of the probe, enabling the two signaling channels to respond differentially to single-base mismatches at different locations. Taking the response to wild-type targets as a reference, synchronized changes in both signals reflect target concentration. A significant decrease in the fluorescence signal alone, with the ECL signal unchanged, indicates that the mismatch occurs within the fluorescence recognition region, whereupon the unaffected ECL channel may serve for quantification. Conversely, when the ECL signal decreases while the fluorescence signal remains stable, the fluorescence channel may serve for quantification. This design enables a single probe to discriminate between wild-type and mutant targets based on the differential responses of the two signaling channels. Our strategy thus provides a new avenue for single-base nucleic acid detection.
